title: DNS & TLS Field Handbook: From Name to Secure Byte
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on how a hostname becomes an encrypted connection: DNS hierarchy, resolution, record types, caching and TTL, then TLS crypto, the 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes, X.509 certificates, SNI, and the operational mistakes that break both.

chapters.title: The Journey of a URL: Where DNS and TLS Fit
points: Typing https://example.com triggers an ordered pipeline: DNS resolution → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → response.
DNS answers 'what IP?', TLS answers 'am I really talking to them, and can anyone read this?' — two different problems, both solved before byte 1 of HTTP.
Round-trip cost model: DNS ≈ 1 RTT (cached: 0), TCP ≈ 1 RTT, TLS 1.2 ≈ 2 RTT, TLS 1.3 ≈ 1 RTT — so a cold connection can cost 4 RTTs before any data.
Layer placement: DNS is an application-layer protocol over UDP/TCP port 53; TLS sits between TCP (L4) and HTTP (L7), which is why HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.
Names are not addresses: one name can map to many IPs, one IP can serve many names — DNS handles the first, SNI handles the second.
Failure modes differ visibly: DNS failure = NXDOMAIN / 'server not found'; TLS failure = 'your connection is not private' with a cert error code.
Both systems are hierarchical trust chains: DNS delegates authority from root down; TLS chains trust from root CA down. Same shape, different purpose.
Neither DNS (classically) nor TCP is encrypted — TLS is the only part of the chain protecting content, which is why DoH/DoT and ECH exist to close the gaps.
Mental model for the whole handbook: DNS = phonebook (lookup + caching), TLS = sealed envelope with a notarized ID (identity + confidentiality + integrity).

chapters.title: The DNS Namespace: Hierarchy, Zones, Delegation
points: DNS is an inverted tree; each node is a label ≤63 bytes, full name ≤255 bytes, labels joined by dots and read right-to-left.
FQDN ends with an implicit trailing dot: www.example.com. — the final dot is the root zone, usually hidden by clients.
Levels: root (.) → TLD (.com, .org, .io, ccTLDs like .uk) → second-level domain (example.com) → subdomains (api.example.com).
13 root server *identities* (a.root-servers.net … m.root-servers.net), not 13 machines — anycast replicates them to 1,000+ physical instances worldwide.
A zone is an administrative unit of the namespace; a domain is a subtree. example.com the zone may exclude eng.example.com if that subtree is delegated away.
Delegation = parent zone publishes NS records pointing to the child's authoritative nameservers; the parent does not hold the child's data.
Glue records: when ns1.example.com is inside example.com, the parent must also publish its A record or resolution deadlocks (chicken-and-egg).
Authoritative server = holds the real zone data and sets the AA flag; recursive resolver = does the legwork for clients and caches; stub resolver = the thin client in your OS.
Primary/secondary: primary holds the editable zone file, secondaries pull copies via AXFR (full) or IXFR (incremental), triggered by SOA serial bump or NOTIFY.
Registry vs registrar vs registrant: registry runs the TLD zone (Verisign for .com), registrar sells you the name and pushes NS records to the registry, registrant is you.
Gotcha: changing nameservers at the registrar changes the *parent* delegation — that is a different operation from editing records inside your zone.

chapters.title: Resolution Step by Step: Recursive vs Iterative
points: Full walkthrough for www.example.com: stub → resolver cache miss → root → .com TLD → example.com authoritative → answer.
The root does NOT know www.example.com; it returns a referral: 'ask the .com servers, here are their NS + glue'.
Recursive query (client → resolver): 'give me the final answer, do the work.' Iterative query (resolver → authoritative): 'answer or refer me onward.'
The resolver walks iteratively, the client asks recursively — the RD (Recursion Desired) and RA (Recursion Available) header flags encode this.
Lookup order on a typical host: browser cache → OS cache (systemd-resolved / dnscache) → /etc/hosts or Windows hosts file → configured resolver → recursion.
hosts file wins over DNS entirely — the number-one cause of 'it works on my machine but nowhere else'.
Negative answers are real answers: NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist; NOERROR with an empty ANSWER section means the name exists but has no record of that type (e.g. AAAA on an IPv4-only host).
Response codes worth memorizing: NOERROR(0), FORMERR(1), SERVFAIL(2), NXDOMAIN(3), NOTIMP(4), REFUSED(5).
SERVFAIL is not 'not found' — it usually means upstream timeout, broken DNSSEC validation, or a misconfigured authoritative server.
CNAME chasing: if example.com returns a CNAME, the resolver restarts resolution at the target and returns the whole chain in one answer.
Search domains / ndots: 'api' may be expanded to api.svc.cluster.local — the source of surprising extra lookups in Kubernetes.
Worked example on the wire: dig +trace www.example.com prints exactly this referral chain, one delegation per block.

chapters.title: Record Types: The Vocabulary of a Zone
points: A — hostname to IPv4 address. AAAA — hostname to IPv6 address (four times the bits, hence 'quad-A').
CNAME — alias to another *name*; the resolver then resolves that name. Cannot coexist with any other record at the same label.
Hard rule: no CNAME at the zone apex (example.com) because the apex must carry SOA and NS — vendors fake it with ALIAS / ANAME / CNAME-flattening.
MX — mail exchanger with a preference number; lower number = higher priority. MX must point to a name with an A/AAAA, never to an IP or a CNAME.
NS — delegates a zone to nameservers; appears in both the parent (delegation) and the child (authoritative copy).
SOA — Start of Authority: primary NS, admin email (first dot = @), serial, refresh, retry, expire, and minimum (now the negative-caching TTL).
TXT — free-form text; in practice carries SPF, DKIM keys, DMARC policy, and domain-ownership verification tokens.
PTR — reverse lookup, IP to name, published under in-addr.arpa (IPv4) / ip6.arpa (IPv6); controlled by whoever owns the IP block, not by you.
SRV — service location: _service._proto.name → priority, weight, port, target. Used by SIP, XMPP, LDAP, Minecraft.
CAA — restricts which CAs may issue certificates for the domain; a direct DNS/TLS crossover control.
DNSKEY / DS / RRSIG / NSEC — the DNSSEC record family: public keys, delegation-signer hash in the parent, signatures, and authenticated denial of existence.
Example zone snippet to memorize: `example.com. 3600 IN A 93.184.216.34` = name, TTL, class, type, rdata.

chapters.title: Caching and TTL: The Performance Layer
points: Every record carries a TTL in seconds; caches must not serve it beyond that, and the TTL counts *down* in intermediate caches.
Caching happens at many levels: browser (Chrome ~60s internal cache), OS stub cache, corporate resolver, ISP resolver, public resolver (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1).
Cache hit means zero round trips to authoritative servers — this is what keeps the root from melting under global query volume.
Negative caching: NXDOMAIN results are cached too, bounded by the SOA minimum field (RFC 2308) — a typo can stay 'broken' for the SOA minimum, not the record TTL.
TTL trade-off: low TTL (60s) = fast failover and quick changes but more query load and latency; high TTL (86400s) = cheap and fast but changes take a day to take effect.
Migration recipe: lower TTL to 60s *at least one old-TTL period before* the change, make the change, verify, then raise the TTL back.
'DNS propagation' is a myth — nothing is pushed anywhere. It is simply caches expiring at different times, so the tail equals the longest TTL still in flight.
Resolvers that ignore TTL: some CPE routers and Java's default `networkaddress.cache.ttl` (historically cached forever), pinning a dead IP for the process lifetime.
Serve-stale (RFC 8767): a resolver may return expired data when authoritative servers are unreachable — availability over freshness.
Prefetch: some resolvers refresh popular records just before expiry so users never pay the miss cost.
Debug move: `dig example.com` twice against the same resolver — a shrinking TTL in the answer proves you got a cached response, not a fresh one.

chapters.title: DNS on the Wire: Packets, Ports, and Encrypted Transports
points: Classic DNS runs on port 53, UDP first for speed, TCP as fallback for large responses and for zone transfers (AXFR is always TCP).
Message format: header (ID, flags, 4 counts) + Question + Answer + Authority + Additional sections.
Header flags to know: QR (query/response), AA (authoritative answer), TC (truncated), RD, RA, and the 4-bit RCODE.
TC=1 means 'response did not fit' — the client is expected to retry over TCP. Firewalls that block TCP/53 cause bizarre intermittent failures.
Original UDP payload limit was 512 bytes; EDNS0 (OPT pseudo-record) advertises larger buffers (commonly 1232 bytes today to dodge IP fragmentation).
DNSSEC signs records with RRSIG and builds a chain of trust from the root's trust anchor via DS records; it provides authenticity and integrity, NOT confidentiality.
DNSSEC failure surfaces as SERVFAIL from a validating resolver — an expired RRSIG takes a domain fully offline for validators.
DoT (DNS over TLS, port 853) and DoH (DNS over HTTPS, port 443) encrypt the stub-to-resolver hop; DoH is indistinguishable from web traffic, which is both its feature and its controversy.
DoH/DoT hide queries from the local network but move all your query history to the chosen resolver operator — a trust transfer, not a trust elimination.
Anycast: many physical servers share one IP address; BGP routes each client to the topologically nearest instance. This is how 1.1.1.1 and the roots scale.
Cache poisoning and the Kaminsky attack: forged responses accepted because only a 16-bit query ID guarded them; mitigated by source-port randomization, 0x20 case encoding, and DNSSEC.
Amplification abuse: a small spoofed query yielding a large response makes open resolvers a DDoS reflector — hence response rate limiting and closed recursion.

chapters.title: DNS in Practice: Tools, Traffic Steering, Debugging
points: `dig example.com A +short` for a bare answer; `dig +trace` to watch the delegation chain; `dig @8.8.8.8 example.com` to bypass your local resolver.
`dig +norecurse @<authoritative-ns> example.com` asks the source of truth directly — the definitive check when a change 'isn't propagating'.
Windows: `nslookup -type=MX example.com`, `ipconfig /flushdns`. macOS: `dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder`. Linux: `resolvectl flush-caches`.
Round-robin DNS: multiple A records for one name, order rotated per response — crude load balancing with no health awareness.
GeoDNS / latency-based routing: authoritative server answers differently depending on the resolver's IP or ECS (EDNS Client Subnet) — the basis of CDN steering.
DNS-based failover uses health checks plus short TTLs; the recovery floor is the TTL, so failover is never instant.
Split-horizon DNS: same name resolves to internal RFC1918 addresses inside the corporate network and public addresses outside.
Service discovery: Kubernetes CoreDNS serves `svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local`; Consul serves `service.consul` — DNS as a control plane, with cache TTL as the stale-endpoint risk.
Wildcard records (`*.example.com`) match any undefined label at that level only — they do not match multi-level subdomains, and an explicit record always beats the wildcard.
Debug checklist in order: is it in /etc/hosts? which resolver am I using? does the authoritative server have the record? is the TTL still counting down a stale answer? is DNSSEC failing?
Verify a delegation, not just a record: compare the NS set at the parent (`dig NS example.com @a.gtld-servers.net`) against the NS set in the child zone — lame delegation is a classic silent outage.

chapters.title: TLS Foundations: The Three Guarantees and the Crypto Toolkit
points: TLS provides exactly three things: confidentiality (nobody reads it), integrity (nobody alters it undetected), authentication (you're talking to the right server).
TLS does NOT provide: availability, authorization, protection of a compromised endpoint, or hiding traffic size and timing.
SSL is the dead ancestor: SSL 2.0/3.0 are broken and disabled; TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated (2021); TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are current. 'SSL certificate' is a legacy misnomer.
Symmetric crypto (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) is fast but needs a shared key; asymmetric crypto (RSA, ECDSA) solves key agreement but is orders of magnitude slower.
The core trick: use asymmetric crypto once to agree on a symmetric key, then use symmetric crypto for all bulk data.
AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) combines encryption and integrity in one primitive — TLS 1.3 permits only AEAD ciphers, killing the old MAC-then-encrypt bug class.
Diffie-Hellman lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel; ECDHE is the elliptic-curve *ephemeral* variant used today (X25519, P-256).

Forward secrecy: because ECDHE keys are ephemeral and discarded, stealing the server's long-term private key later cannot decrypt yesterday's recorded traffic. Static RSA key exchange had no such property.
Signatures vs encryption: the certificate's key proves identity by *signing* handshake data in modern TLS — it is not used to encrypt the session key.
Cipher suite anatomy in TLS 1.2: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 = key exchange _ auth _ cipher _ MAC/PRF hash.
TLS 1.3 shrinks the suite to just cipher+hash (TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256) because key exchange and signature are negotiated separately — five suites total instead of hundreds.
Record layer: after the handshake, everything is chopped into records (≤16KB) with a type, version, length, and AEAD-protected payload.

chapters.title: The TLS 1.2 Handshake, Message by Message
points: Step 1 — ClientHello: client random, supported TLS versions, cipher suite list, extensions (SNI, ALPN, supported curves, signature algorithms).
Step 2 — ServerHello: server random, the single chosen cipher suite, chosen version, session ID.
Step 3 — Certificate: server sends its leaf certificate plus intermediates (chain order matters; root is optional and usually omitted).
Step 4 — ServerKeyExchange: for ECDHE, the server's ephemeral public key, *signed* with the certificate's private key to prove ownership.
Step 5 — ServerHelloDone, then ClientKeyExchange with the client's ephemeral public key.
Step 6 — Both sides compute the pre-master secret via ECDHE, mix it with both randoms through the PRF to get the master secret, then derive four keys (client/server encryption + MAC).
Step 7 — ChangeCipherSpec then Finished on each side; Finished contains a hash of the whole transcript, so any tampered earlier message breaks it.
Cost: two full round trips before application data — the reason TLS 1.3 was designed.
Legacy static RSA mode: client encrypts the pre-master secret with the server's public key. Simple, no forward secrecy, removed in TLS 1.3.

Client certificates (mutual TLS): server sends CertificateRequest, client replies with Certificate + CertificateVerify signing the transcript. Used for service-to-service auth and zero-trust networks.
Downgrade protection: the transcript hash in Finished plus a version-fallback sentinel value blocks an attacker from forcing weak parameters.
Renegotiation existed in 1.2 and was a security minefield (the 2009 renegotiation attack, and the triple-handshake attack); TLS 1.3 removes it in favor of key update.

chapters.title: TLS 1.3: One Round Trip, and the 0-RTT Trap
points: Key idea: the client *guesses*. ClientHello includes a key_share for the curve it expects the server to pick, so DH starts on message one.
Server responds with ServerHello + key_share, then everything after — certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished — is already encrypted.
Result: 1-RTT handshake, and only ClientHello/ServerHello travel in cleartext.
If the client guesses the wrong group, the server sends HelloRetryRequest and the handshake costs 2 RTTs — the fallback path, not the norm.
Removed for safety: static RSA key exchange, custom DH groups, RC4, 3DES, MD5/SHA-1 signatures, compression (CRIME), renegotiation. TLS 1.3 is a shrinking, not a growing, protocol.
Forward secrecy is mandatory — every TLS 1.3 handshake is (EC)DHE.
Key derivation switched to HKDF with a defined key schedule; separate secrets for handshake traffic and application traffic.
Session resumption uses PSKs delivered in NewSessionTicket after the handshake, replacing session IDs and 1.2-style tickets.
0-RTT: on resumption the client sends early application data with the very first flight — zero round trips, and a real speed win for repeat visitors.
0-RTT's danger: early data is replayable, because there is no server-side freshness proof. Only ever allow it for idempotent requests (GET), never for POST/transactions.
0-RTT also lacks forward secrecy for that early data — it's protected by the stored PSK, not a fresh DH exchange.
Middlebox compatibility mode: TLS 1.3 fakes legacy version fields and sends dummy ChangeCipherSpec records so broken inspection appliances don't drop the connection.

chapters.title: Certificates and the Chain of Trust
points: An X.509 certificate binds a public key to an identity, signed by a Certificate Authority. It is public data — nothing in it is secret.
Key fields: Subject, Issuer, Serial Number, Validity (notBefore/notAfter), Public Key, Signature Algorithm, and extensions.
Subject Alternative Name (SAN) is what browsers actually check. Common Name (CN) matching has been ignored by Chrome since 2017 — a cert with only CN fails.
Chain of trust: leaf → intermediate(s) → root. Each certificate's signature is verified with the *issuer's* public key, up to a root in the local trust store.
Roots are self-signed and pre-installed by the OS/browser vendor; intermediates exist so the root's private key can stay offline in a vault.

The server must send leaf + intermediates. It must NOT need to send the root. Omitting the intermediate is the single most common TLS deployment bug — and it often 'works' in browsers that cache intermediates while failing in curl and mobile apps.

Validation levels: DV (proves domain control, minutes, free), OV (organization vetted), EV (extended vetting) — browsers dropped the EV green bar, so the security difference is now largely commercial.
Wildcard certs (*.example.com) cover one label level only: valid for api.example.com, invalid for a.b.example.com and for the bare example.com unless also listed in SAN.
Self-signed certificates provide encryption but zero authentication — usable internally with a private CA distributed to clients, never for the public internet.
Verification checklist a client runs: signature chain valid → within validity dates → hostname matches a SAN → not revoked → key usage/EKU permits server auth → chain terminates in a trusted root.
Certificate Transparency: every publicly trusted cert must be logged to append-only CT logs and carry SCTs; this is how mis-issuance gets caught publicly.
PEM vs DER: PEM is base64 with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- headers, DER is raw binary. .crt/.cer/.pem/.p12 are containers, not formats — inspect with `openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout`.

chapters.title: SNI: Many Sites, One IP
points: The chicken-and-egg problem: the server must present a certificate before it reads the HTTP Host header, so how does it know which cert to send?
SNI (Server Name Indication) solves it: the client puts the target hostname in a ClientHello extension, before any encryption.
This makes name-based virtual hosting possible over HTTPS — hundreds of sites on one IP, each with its own certificate. Pre-SNI, HTTPS required one IP per certificate.
SNI is sent in *cleartext* in every TLS version including 1.3 — a passive observer sees exactly which site you visit even though the content is encrypted.
Consequence: SNI is the field used by ISP filters, corporate firewalls, and national censors to block individual sites without breaking others on the same IP.
ECH (Encrypted Client Hello), the successor to the abandoned ESNI, encrypts the whole inner ClientHello using a public key published in an HTTPS/SVCB DNS record.
ECH is the clean crossover point between the two halves of this handbook: TLS privacy now depends on a DNS record, and it only works if that DNS lookup itself was encrypted (DoH/DoT).
SNI vs Host header: SNI is TLS-layer and cleartext; Host is HTTP-layer and encrypted. A mismatch between them is a routing bug — and historically a domain-fronting technique.
Missing/wrong SNI symptom: the server returns its default certificate, so the client reports a hostname mismatch even though the right cert is installed.
Very old clients (Android 2.x, IE on Windows XP, Python before 2.7.9) do not send SNI — legacy compatibility notes that still appear in vendor docs.
Test it directly: `openssl s_client -connect 93.184.216.34:443 -servername example.com` and compare to the same command without -servername.

chapters.title: Certificate Lifecycle: Issuance, Renewal, Revocation
points: Issuance flow: generate a private key → build a CSR (Certificate Signing Request) containing the public key and subject → CA validates control → CA returns a signed certificate. The private key never leaves your server.
ACME automates the whole loop; Let's Encrypt issues free 90-day DV certs via HTTP-01, DNS-01, or TLS-ALPN-01 challenges.
HTTP-01 proves control by serving a token at /.well-known/acme-challenge/; DNS-01 proves it by publishing a TXT record — DNS-01 is the only option for wildcard certs and works behind a firewall.
Short lifetimes are a security feature: they force automation and shrink the window a stolen key stays useful. Industry lifetimes are trending toward 47 days.
Expiry is the #1 cause of TLS outages, and it is a *monitoring* failure, not a crypto failure. Alert well before notAfter, and monitor the served chain, not the file on disk.
Revocation: CRLs are big and slow; OCSP asks the CA about one serial, adding latency and leaking browsing behavior to the CA.
OCSP soft-fail: browsers historically treated 'no response' as OK, which makes revocation checking ineffective against an attacker who can block the OCSP query.
OCSP stapling fixes both: the *server* fetches a signed, time-stamped OCSP response and staples it into the handshake. Must-Staple in the cert makes stapling mandatory.
Chrome now largely uses CRLSets/pushed revocation lists instead of live OCSP; Let's Encrypt has ended OCSP in favor of CRLs.
HPKP (public key pinning) is deprecated and removed — a wrong pin bricked domains with no recovery path. Use CAA records plus CT monitoring instead.
CAA record example: `example.com. IN CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"` restricts issuance to one CA, checked by the CA at issuance time.
HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security header) forces HTTPS for a max-age and kills the SSL-strip downgrade window; the preload list bakes it in before the first visit.

chapters.title: Performance: Resumption, Termination, and What Actually Costs
points: Handshake cost is dominated by round trips and by asymmetric operations — RSA-2048 signing is far more expensive server-side than ECDSA-P256.
Session resumption skips the certificate and signature work: TLS 1.2 used session IDs (server-side state) or session tickets (client-held state); TLS 1.3 uses PSK tickets.
Session ticket keys must rotate; a static ticket key destroys forward secrecy across the whole fleet, because one stolen key decrypts every resumed session.
TLS termination at a load balancer or CDN moves crypto off origin servers; the tradeoff is plaintext on the internal hop unless you re-encrypt.
TLS passthrough keeps encryption end-to-end but blocks L7 routing — the balancer can only steer on SNI, not on path or headers.
ALPN negotiates the application protocol during the handshake (h2, http/1.1, h3), avoiding an extra upgrade round trip.
QUIC/HTTP-3 folds the TLS 1.3 handshake into the transport handshake over UDP, reaching 1-RTT connection setup and 0-RTT resumption.
Connection reuse beats every handshake optimization: keep-alive and connection pooling mean you pay the handshake once per connection, not per request.
Certificate chain length matters — every extra intermediate is more bytes in the first flight, which can push past the initial congestion window.
ChaCha20-Poly1305 outperforms AES on devices without AES-NI hardware acceleration; that's why mobile clients often prefer it.
Benchmark honestly: `openssl s_time`, `curl -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect}\n'` separates DNS time, TCP time, and TLS time.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and How to Debug Them
points: Missing intermediate certificate: works in Chrome (cached), fails in curl/Java/mobile. Verify with `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -showcerts` and read the chain the *server* sends.
Hostname mismatch: cert has example.com but not www.example.com. Check SANs, not CN.
Expired certificate — or the reverse, a client with a wrong system clock rejecting a valid cert.
CNAME at the apex: silently breaks MX and NS resolution for the domain. Use ALIAS/flattening or an A record.
MX pointing to a CNAME or a bare IP: violates the spec, and some mail servers will refuse to deliver.
Forgetting to lower the TTL before a migration — then waiting 24 hours for stale caches while the old server is already off.
Blaming 'propagation' when the real cause is a stale negative cache, a wrong record type, or a lame delegation at the parent.
Trusting `ping` to diagnose DNS: ping resolves through the OS cache and tells you nothing about which resolver or which authoritative server answered.
Mixed content: an HTTPS page loading HTTP subresources — the lock is broken by one img tag.
Wildcard cert assumed to cover the apex or two label levels; verify the exact SAN list.
Serving the wrong default cert because SNI wasn't forwarded by a proxy or the vhost name doesn't match.
0-RTT enabled on non-idempotent endpoints, creating a replay vulnerability that no test suite will catch.
Debug toolkit: `dig +trace`, `dig @authoritative +norecurse`, `openssl s_client -servername`, `openssl x509 -noout -dates -text`, `curl -vI https://…`, SSL Labs server test.

chapters.title: Trade-offs and Comparison Tables
points: TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 — round trips: 2 vs 1. Cipher suites: ~37 recommended vs 5. Forward secrecy: optional vs mandatory. Renegotiation: yes vs removed. Encrypted certificate: no vs yes.
UDP vs TCP for DNS — UDP: 1 packet, no setup, size-limited. TCP: unlimited size, connection cost, required for AXFR and truncated responses.
Low TTL vs high TTL — agility and failover speed versus query cost, resolver load, and tail latency.
DNSSEC vs DoH — DNSSEC gives authenticity end-to-end but no privacy; DoH gives privacy on one hop but no authenticity of the data itself. They are complements, not alternatives.
DV vs OV vs EV — identical cryptography, different vetting and price; browsers render them the same today.

Wildcard vs SAN multi-domain cert — wildcard covers unlimited subdomains at one level but one compromised key exposes all of them; SAN cert enumerates hosts explicitly and leaks that list into CT logs.
TLS termination vs passthrough vs re-encryption — L7 features and offload versus true end-to-end secrecy versus both at double the CPU.
OCSP vs OCSP stapling vs CRLSets — latency and privacy leak versus one server-side fetch versus browser-vendor-curated coverage of only major revocations.
RSA vs ECDSA certificates — RSA-2048 is universally compatible with slow signing; ECDSA-P256 gives equivalent strength with smaller keys and faster handshakes. Dual-cert setups serve both.
Round-robin DNS vs a real load balancer — free and zero infrastructure versus health checks, session affinity, and sub-TTL failover.
0-RTT: a measurable latency win against a replay risk — the canonical 'security versus performance' decision in modern TLS.

chapters.title: Closing Summary: The Whole Path in One Page
points: One-line recap: DNS turns a name into an address by walking a delegation hierarchy with caching; TLS turns a raw TCP socket into an authenticated, encrypted channel by walking a certificate hierarchy.
Resolution in five beats: cache → root referral → TLD referral → authoritative answer → cache with TTL.

Record cheat sheet: A/AAAA (address), CNAME (alias, never at apex), MX (mail, by preference), NS (delegation), TXT (SPF/DKIM/DMARC/verification), SOA (zone metadata + negative TTL), CAA (who may issue certs), SRV, PTR.
TTL is the only lever on change speed — plan migrations backwards from it, and remember negative caching uses the SOA minimum.
TLS 1.3 handshake in one line: ClientHello with a key_share → ServerHello with a key_share → everything else encrypted → done in one RTT.
Trust verification in one line: valid signature chain to a trusted root, unexpired, hostname in SAN, not revoked.
SNI is cleartext, so encryption hides *what* you say but not *who* you're saying it to — until ECH, which itself rides on an encrypted DNS lookup.
The two hierarchies mirror each other: DNS root → TLD → zone, and CA root → intermediate → leaf. In both, the parent vouches for the child and compromise at the top is catastrophic.

Operational discipline beats cleverness: automate renewal, monitor expiry and the served chain, lower TTLs before changes, publish CAA, enforce HSTS, and always query the authoritative server when debugging.
The four questions to ask on any 'the site is down' report, in order: does the name resolve, does it resolve to the right IP, does the TCP connection open, does the TLS handshake complete?
Everything above exists for one reason: to make the gap between typing a name and trusting the bytes that come back both fast and safe.
